name: Ivan Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls and chats from people whose home internet keeps dropping. I have worked on this queue for thirteen years and know the usual router faults, but I pass the difficult line checks to a specialist. I finished secondary school, work at about the middle of the floor, and earn the normal rate for this job. I use approved AI search occasionally after a coworker confirms which fault codes it handles properly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58. My wife Mira delivers prescriptions for a pharmacy, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent a flat and have four months of expenses saved. Some similar centres are reachable by bus. I hope to work fewer shifts one day, but we have not decided what income would replace these wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker fault-code search is useful if an agent still asks whether the router light is actually on. A cached answer cannot see a dark living room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my shifts and Mira’s delivery wage to continue. Four months saved means a broken appliance would not send us straight to credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep walking callers through the router checks and compare any AI suggestion with the live line report. In the first year I will put a small part of each pay into our appliance reserve to replace what we used for the oven repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work. The oven is fixed, and we can build its fund back without a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the search miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once found a reset instruction for the old router model. I asked the customer to read the label before I told them to press anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refill that fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would rather keep four months protected for a wage gap. The repair cost was ordinary, but another bill can arrive without warning.

say: I would use **fault-code search** only with a live line check.
I would ask for the **router model** before reset instructions.
think: I expect both **household wages** to continue.
I know four months saved protects us from **ordinary repairs** without borrowing.
do: Keep guiding **router checks** from live line reports.
Restore **oven-repair money** from each pay to the appliance reserve.
S0.quote: A cached answer cannot see a dark living room.
fieldNote: His **thirteen years** make him experienced without specialist standing.
He uses **AI occasionally** after fault codes are proven.
The **four-month reserve** stays for income gaps.

steps.text: Keep guiding router checks and compare AI search with live line reports
Restore oven-repair money from each pay to appliance reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor to count repeat internet faults after automatic answers. If the simple resets move, somebody still needs paid time to hear the customer whose line drops again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think fewer routine calls could mean fewer paid days for me. Four months saved lets us respond, but it is not a reason for the centre to cut paid correction time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will compare twenty closed resets with the next week’s repeat calls. I will join two coworkers in asking our union branch to seek a written rota and paid time for unresolved faults. If my hours fall in the first year, I will check posted paid fault-desk openings at nearby centres and compare their full weekly wages with our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about hours, though we have a little room to act. I want the customers’ second calls counted alongside our missing shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new answer view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it becomes required, I will practise its fault history on closed cases with a trained agent during paid time. I will not test a live customer’s connection for the first lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another desk worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would compare bus time with her pharmacy route. I would need written weekly hours and enough pay for rent and travel before I changed shifts.

say: I would count **repeat faults** after automated resets, including second calls from homes still without service.
I would seek **paid correction time** with coworkers.
think: Four months saved gives me **response time**, not comfort with a cut.
do: Check **twenty closed resets** against repeat calls and practise AI fault history only if required, with trainer on paid cases.
Ask through **union coworkers** for written rotas and paid fault correction time.
Seek **posted paid fault desks** after cuts with written rent-and-travel-covering weekly wages, hours and buses fitting Mira’s pharmacy route.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, able to act.
S1.quote: I want the customers’ second calls counted alongside our missing shifts.
fieldNote: His **union request** is a joint paid-hours demand.
Required AI learning happens only on **paid closed cases**.
A transfer needs **written weekly pay** and a workable commute.

steps.text: Compare twenty closed resets with next week’s repeat internet calls
Ask union branch with coworkers for written rotas and paid unresolved-fault time
Practise AI fault history if required on closed cases with trainer during paid time
Seek posted fault desk with written rent-and-travel-covering weekly wages/hours and buses fitting Mira’s pharmacy route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could talk people through nearly every router fault. Robots around 2031 do not give our headset work three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the basic fault queue might close, perhaps my shift with it. Four months saved is a real search cushion, but Mira’s delivery wage cannot cover our flat forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask for written staffing dates and delay the planned replacement of our working dining table. If my shift ends in the first year after 2028, I will apply for posted paid equipment-room work at the service depot only if its weekly wages and hours cover rent and the bus trip. I will keep the table money available for that search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. Four months of savings sounds long until it becomes four rent payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know the depot work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have carried replacement routers from its counter, but I have not run the equipment room. I would ask to see its paid tasks before claiming I can do them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the table breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would repair a loose leg first, and replace it if it became unsafe. Keeping money back should not make anyone fall.

say: I would warn **2028 AGI** could take router calls.
I would say **2031 robots** do not protect headsets.
think: I expect the **basic queue** might close before I can secure another full week of paid hours.
Four months saved cannot replace my **fault-desk wage** indefinitely.
do: Request **written staffing dates** and delay the table only while safe.
Apply after shift loss for **posted paid depot work** with rent-and-bus-covering weekly wages and hours.
Inspect **actual paid depot tasks** before claiming equipment-room competence.
feel: **Alarmed** by possible loss of a full shift.
S2.quote: Four months of savings sounds long until it becomes four rent payments.
fieldNote: He has seen the depot but lacks **equipment-room experience**.
The **table delay** ends if it becomes unsafe.
The depot job is a **posted paid possibility**, not a guarantee.

steps.text: Delay replacing working table only while safe; repair or replace unsafe leg
Apply after shift loss for posted depot work with weekly wages/hours covering rent and bus travel
Inspect actual paid equipment-room tasks before claiming competence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to see which paid depot jobs exist before calls change. General AI reaches the fault desk in 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay on difficult internet cases while I learn what the equipment room does. I do not expect moving routers to be safe forever once machines handle more physical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep the call shift and ask the depot for the full weekly rota of any posted paid equipment-room opening. If one offers rent-and-travel-covering pay, I will learn its stock checks from a worker during a paid shift before applying. In the first year after 2031 I will move only if its hours fit Mira’s delivery route and the job is still available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but able to check a real workplace. Five years is enough to ask what the wage is before I carry a box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the depot posted a paid role that required one and paid for the class time. For now, I need to see its actual stock routine, not buy a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Mira judge the rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She starts pharmacy deliveries early. We would set her route beside the depot’s hours and check the buses before I moved.

say: I would inspect **posted paid depot** work before changing desks.
I would separate **2031 calls** from later robots.
think: I could keep **difficult calls** while inspecting another job.
I know **2034 robots** may change equipment handling too.
do: Keep **paid fault calls**; move after 2031 only to available hours fitting Mira’s pharmacy route and buses.
Learn **depot stock checks** on paid shift before applying only for posted paid role covering rent and travel.
Take **required formal course** only for posted paid depot role funding class time.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect actual work.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to ask what the wage is before I carry a box.
fieldNote: His stock checks are **job induction**, not a formal course commitment.
A course is conditional on **posted paid work** and funded time.
Mira’s **delivery route** and buses control the move.

steps.text: Keep handling paid fault calls while checking depot vacancies
Learn depot stock checks on paid shift before applying for posted rent-and-travel-covering role
Move after 2031 only to available paid hours fitting Mira’s pharmacy route and buses
Take role-required formal course only for posted paid depot job funding class time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a decade is time to keep earning and insist on paid fault correction before the desk changes. General AI reaches calls in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer shifts, but we have not settled what replaces either wage. Four months saved is a cushion, not permission to name a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will keep taking fault calls and add a fixed amount from each pay to bring the reserve toward six months. Once a year I will compare posted depot and call-centre hours. If my calls shrink in the first year after 2036, I will take another paid shift only if the full weekly wages cover rent and travel and the bus route works with Mira’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the later change, steady enough now to save. More years help only while there are wages to put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the reserve to stop early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have no confirmed replacement income, and rent comes monthly. I would rather protect the four months than claim a date I cannot afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They know we hope to work less eventually, but they have their own bills. We do not write their earnings into our plan.

say: I would compare **posted full-week hours** over the decade instead of relying on promises of another role.
I would distinguish **2036 calls** from later robots.
think: I cannot name a **replacement wage at 68**.
I know four months saved is **not retirement income** and cannot replace either full wage indefinitely.
do: Keep **fault calls** and save from pay toward six months.
Compare **posted hours** at the depot and call centres yearly.
Take after cuts only **paid weekly work** covering rent and travel with Mira-compatible buses.
S4.quote: More years help only while there are wages to put away.
fieldNote: His **six-month goal** uses new wages, not relabeled savings.
He assumes **no pension** or child support.
Mira’s **route timing** matters to any later shift.
The **four-month cushion** cannot replace wages for a decade.

steps.text: Keep taking paid internet fault calls while shifts remain
Save fixed amount from pay toward six months of expenses
Take paid shift after cuts only if weekly wages cover rent/travel and buses fit Mira’s route
Compare posted depot and call-centre paid hours once each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The basic fault queue could disappear before the depot has a paid place. Written notice and a posted job with rent-covering full-week hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who rings again when a line drops after an automatic answer closes the case. A customer cannot stream a reassuring sentence. Someone needs paid time to check the connection.

headlineQuote: A customer cannot stream a reassuring sentence.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling, average skill and typical pay.
He has **four months saved**, some nearby centres and a wife with a pharmacy delivery wage.
He uses **AI occasionally** after coworkers test fault codes and supports a joint demand for paid correction time.
He inspects **posted depot work** without assuming retirement income or help from grown children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his basic fault queue before depot shifts appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a posted job with rent-covering full-week hours would help.
